newsitem.title: USA: 25 years on, Watergate a cancer on U.S. presidency.
newsitem.headline: 25 years on, Watergate a cancer on U.S. presidency.

text.p: Twenty-five years after a botched burglary started an avalanche that ultimately swept Richard Nixon from the White House, the Watergate scandal is still a cancer on the U.S. presidency.

As America marks the ignominious anniversary of the worst political scandal in U.S. history, those who lived through it say it left a weakened presidency, a public cynical and distrusting of politicians and a press that goes for the jugular at the slighest excuse.

"Along with the Vietnam War, it diminished the presidency. The awesome respect the office had been given historically is not there anymore, and I don't know if it's possible to get it back," retired Congressman Don Edwards said in an interview.

Edwards, a senior member of the House of Representatives committee that probed the scandal and recommended that Nixon be removed from office, said it had also weakened confidence in the integrity of the Justice Department.
That legacy is apparent in the inevitable clamour, following the Watergate precedent, for an independent prosecutor whenever a high official is accused of wrongdoing.

Three of Nixon's five successors -- Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush and Democrat Bill Clinton -- have had to live with independent prosecutors, Reagan and Bush for a foreign policy controversy called the Iran-Contra affair and Clinton for the Whitewater banking and ethics flap.
"We ought to insist whenever we can that the Department of Justice be allowed to do its work. It's wrong to automatically assume a conflict of interest," Edwards said.

The scandal also triggered campaign financing reforms that have since been blamed for encouraging abuses, like Clinton's freewheeling quest for limitless "soft money" contributions to fund his drive for re-election in 1996.

Under Watergate-inspired regulations, wealthy donors, corporations and labour unions can get around federal limits of $1,000 to individual candidates by donating as much money as they want to the Republican or Democratic parties.
"They (the reforms) cleaned up maybe two elections, and then politicians found a way to get around them," political analyst Stephen Hess of Brookings Institution said.

But Watergate also had a positive effect, leading to liberalised access to government documents of all sorts, including thed documents that recently led to the exposure of the Swiss banking and Nazi gold scandal.

It was John Dean, the Nixon aide turned chief accuser, who first warned of the corrosive effects of what started as a break-in at the Democratic Party's national headquarters at the Watergate office and apartment complex on June 17, 1972.
At a May 21, 1973 meeting in the Oval Office with Nixon and some of Nixon's top advisers, Dean called Watergate "a cancer within the presidency," but his warning was ignored.

Efforts by the Republican White House to cover up the fact the five men caught in the act of breaking and entering worked for Nixon's re-election campaign led to exposure of a massive conspiracy and assorted abuses of power that forced the 37th president to resign under threat of impeachment.

In a book called "In the Arena," Nixon wrote, "In retrospect, I should have set a higher standard for the conduct of the people who participated in my campaign and administration. I should have established a moral tone that would have made such actions unthinkable. I did not."
The disgraced former president said he had "played by the rules of politics as I found them. Not taking a higher road than my predecessors and my adversaries was my central mistake," he said.
Nixon's Attorney General, John Mitchell, and several top White House aides were convicted of Watergate-related crimes and went to jail.

A federal grand jury named Nixon himself as an unindicted co-conspirator. Nixon spent years trying to redeem his good name and was regarded as a foreign policy elder statesman at the time of his death in 1994 and had established a close relationship with President Clinton, who sought his advice more often than Presidents Reagan and Bush did.

Watergate "caused a real souring of the political system. Afterwards, we see a significant increase in negative public attitudes toward government in survey data," said Fred Greenstein, a Princeton University political scientist.

The scandal was uncovered largely as as a result of dogged investigative journalism by Washington Post reporters Robert Woodward and Carl Bernstein. Ever since, U.S. journalism has been "more intrusive with fewer boundaries and less ready to be positive" in covering the presidency, Greenstein said.
Edwards, a California Democrat who served in Congress for more than three decades, said there was one bright aspect of Watergate -- it showed the strength of the U.S. Constitution.

"The country held together. The Constitution worked. In most countries, there would have been bloodshed because of the power at stake but it was remarkable how the American people handled this," he said.
